newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Germany,"Club Med" miss same EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Germany,"Club Med" miss same EMU criteria.

text.p: Germany, Austria and Belgium, three of Europe's strongest economies, are likely to fall short of the criteria required for a single currency in exactly the same categories as their poorer relations Italy, Portugal and Spain, according to a Reuters poll published on Monday.

The first of a series of quarterly polls on how European countries are shaping up for monetary union show the "Club Med" countries will need to adopt stringent measures to come anywhere near the budget deficit and debt criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) set under the Maastricht Treaty.
Yet in the strictest sense, Germany, Austria and Belgium would also struggle to meet the same criteria.

Fortunately for them, all the Maastricht terms are subject to interpretation, which many economists reckon will be loose to allow the union to go ahead. Another Reuters poll has indicated they are almost certain to be in the first wave of EMU anyhow.
"(The European Commission) are not going to throw Germany out on its debt or deficit level," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi in London.
The extent to which countries overshoot the criteria, as well as stability considerations, is crucial.
"Italy's debt numbers are horrendous - twice as bad as they are in Germany," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America in London.

The Maastricht Treaty states that total debt should account for no more than 60 percent of GDP. The poll predicted Germany would just fail to meet the required level at between 60 and 65 percent while Spain's debt would come in at between 65 and 70 percent of GDP.
In Austria, Belgium, Italy and Portugal, debt was expected to come in at over 70 percent of GDP in 1997.
The Reuters poll did not ask participants to forecast exact levels, but earlier this month the European Commission forecast debt for both Italy and Belgium at more than 120 percent of GDP.

The budget deficit to GDP ratio should be no more than three percent. The poll showed that this ratio would probably fall between 3.0 and 3.5 percent in Germany, Austria and Belgium as well as Portugal and Spain in 1997 and between 3.5 and 4.0 percent in Italy.

Italy, the only one of the six countries not currently a member of the Exchange Rate Mechanism, looks set to join before 1996 is over and thus fulfill another EMU requirement, according to the Reuters survey. In theory, this would put all six countries level in terms of convergence criteria pass and fail.
But economists said that Germany's ranking alongside the "Club Med" countries was illusory.

While the southern fringe countries are taking stringent measures to meet the criteria, their historical lack of stability means the financial community tends to look on their efforts less favourably.
"The big worry as far as the markets are concerned is that they've yet to go through a full period of stability," said Bank of America's Hawkins.
Economists also doubt whether the results of their efforts will be durable.
And where Germany has resisted the temptation to indulge in "creative accounting" to meet the criteria, other countries have taken one-off measures.

"Germany, if it fails, will fail without having fudged. It will have failed by being completely honest and without any manipulation of its own statistics," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO in the Netherlands.

The German government has been commended for sticking to its guns in a recession-hit economy with unemployment at record highs, faced with an electorate upset at a reduction in perks and a worsening tax burden.
Despite its sickly debt and deficit figures, some economists reckon Italy is now taking the right medicine.
"If Italy does qualify and makes the necessary changes, they will be genuine, probably structural changes," said Venables.
Yamaichi's Richardson said that a lower cost of borrowing, possible because of lower inflation in Italy, would help to reduce the deficit. "It's not all window-dressing," he said.
